mainTopic: The end of the ten trials in the desert, and the severity, remedy and definition of לשון הרע
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא's list of the ten times the Jewish people tested הקב״ה in the desert: two with the מן, two with the quail, the golden calf, and the spies in מדבר פארן. Then the גמרא turns to a long series of teachings on how serious לשון הרע is. It is compared to denying God, it brings נגעים, it raises sins to the heavens, it deserves stoning, and God cannot share the world with the one who speaks it. רבי חמא ברבי חנינא gives a remedy: a תלמיד חכם should learn Torah and an עם הארץ should humble himself. רבי אחא ברבי חנינא says these only prevent the sin and cannot fix it after it is spoken. The school of רבי ישמעאל teaches that לשון הרע equals עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים together. A chain of פסוקים then shows that the tongue kills like a hand, like an arrow, and from heaven to earth. Finally, רבא, אביי and רבה argue about what counts as לישנא בישא, including whether speech said in front of its subject is included. A new statement begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The two trials with the מן
steps.stepSummary: The two trials with the מן were disobeying 'do not go out' on שבת and disobeying 'do not leave any over.'
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said 'do not go out' to collect מן on שבת, and people went out. He said 'do not leave any over' until morning, and people left some over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining which two events count as the 'two trials with the מן' in the list of ten trials.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each trial is shown in two parts: what משה commanded and how some people broke it. The first is about collecting מן on שבת. The second is about keeping מן overnight when told not to.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not go out (to collect מן on שבת)
Do not leave any over (until morning)
A test or trial; here, the people testing הקב״ה

phrases.english: "Do not go out" and they went out;
phrases.notes: This is about going out to collect מן on שבת (שמות 16).

phrases.english: "Do not leave any over" and they left some over.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַל תֵּצֵאוּ וַיֵּצְאוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier explanation of the ברייתא's list of ten trials, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two trials with the מן were going out on שבת against the command, and leaving מן overnight against the command.

steps.title: Two trials with the quail, starting with the first
steps.stepSummary: There were two trials with quail, on two separate occasions. The first is the complaint about the 'meat pots' of מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two trials with the quail: the first time quail came and the second time quail came. The first quail: 'when we sat by the pot of meat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the 'two trials with the quail' happened on two separate occasions. It then points to the פסוק for the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quail came twice, once in ספר שמות and once in ספר במדבר, and each coming followed a complaint. The first complaint was the people longing for the meat they had in מצרים.

keyTerms.meaning: Quail, the birds הקב״ה sent as meat
The pot of meat (that they remembered from מצרים)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two quail events. The first is in שמות 16, right before the מן started. The second is in במדבר 11, much later.

phrases.english: Two with the quail:
with the first quail and with the second quail.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is the corrected wording, so read it as 'with the first quail.'

phrases.english: The first quail:
"When we sat by the pot of meat."

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁנַיִם בַּשְּׂלָיו בִּשְׂלָיו רִאשׁוֹן וּבִשְׂלָיו שֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next pair in the list of ten trials.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The quail trials were two separate events. The first was the complaint about the meat pots of מצרים.

steps.title: The second quail trial
steps.stepSummary: The second quail trial is the complaint started by the mixed multitude (אספסוף).
steps.simpleTranslation: The second quail: 'And the mixed multitude that was among them' craved meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the פסוק for the second time the people complained and quail was sent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the episode in ספר במדבר, where the אספסוף started craving meat and the people cried along with them. It counts as its own separate trial.

keyTerms.meaning: The mixed multitude, a crowd of non-Jews who left מצרים with the Jewish people

phrases.english: The second quail:
"And the mixed multitude that was among them."

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׂלָיו שֵׁנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the pair of quail trials begun in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second quail trial was the complaint of the אספסוף in במדבר 11.

steps.title: The golden calf and מדבר פארן
steps.stepSummary: The last two trials, the golden calf and מדבר פארן, need no proof because the Torah tells them openly.
steps.simpleTranslation: With the עגל, it is as written. In מדבר פארן, it is as written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list of ten trials. It says the last two are clear from the Torah itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the earlier trials the גמרא had to show which פסוק matched each one. The עגל and the spies in מדבר פארן are famous, openly told stories, so all it says is 'as it is written.'

keyTerms.meaning: As it is (as the Torah plainly tells it)
The wilderness of Paran, where the spies were sent out

steps.whatToRemember: The ten trials are: two at the sea, two with water, two with the מן, two with quail, one with the golden calf, and one in מדבר פארן (the spies).

phrases.english: With the calf, it is as it is written;
in the wilderness of Paran, it is as it is written.
phrases.notes: This is the story of the spies (במדבר 13–14).

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵגֶל כִּדְאִיתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the list after the quail trials.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All ten trials are now matched to the Torah. The last two need no extra proof because the Torah tells them plainly.

steps.title: God guarded the tongue with special protections
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי יוסי בן זימרא, explains a פסוק in תהלים. God tells the tongue: I made you lie flat, kept you inside, and surrounded you with two walls. What more can I do to stop you from speaking deceit?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי בן זימרא: What does the verse mean, 'What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done for you, deceitful tongue'? God said to the tongue: All of a person's limbs stand upright, but you lie flat. All of a person's limbs are on the outside, but you are inside. And not only that, I surrounded you with two walls, one of bone and one of flesh. What more can be given to you, and what more can be done for you, deceitful tongue?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new section on לשון הרע by explaining a פסוק as God speaking to the tongue. God lists all the protections He built around it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק's question 'what more can be done for you' is read as a complaint from God. The tongue was given every possible barrier: it lies down, it is hidden inside, and it is walled in by teeth and lips. So a person who still speaks deceit has broken through all of these barriers.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but even more

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן זִימְרָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done for you,
deceitful tongue"?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַלָּשׁוֹן:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the tongue:
All of a person's limbs are upright,
but you lie flat.
All of a person's limbs are on the outside,
but you are inside.
And not only that,
I surrounded you with two walls,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת שֶׁל עֶצֶם וְאַחַת שֶׁל בָּשָׂר,
phrases.english: one of bone and one of flesh.
phrases.notes: The bone wall is the teeth, and the flesh wall is the lips.

phrases.english: "What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done for you,
deceitful tongue"?
phrases.notes: Now the same פסוק reads as God asking what more He could possibly do to hold the tongue back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן זִימְרָא: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of the ten trials in the מדבר and returns to the theme of לשון הרע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God placed the tongue lying down, inside the body, and behind two walls (teeth and lips), so there is nothing more that can be done to keep it from speaking deceit.

steps.title: Speaking לשון הרע is like denying God
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בן זימרא, quoted by רבי יוחנן, teaches that one who speaks לשון הרע is like someone who denies God. The proof is a פסוק where people boast about their tongues and ask, 'Who is master over us?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי בן זימרא: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע is as if he denied the fundamental belief in God, as it says: 'Who have said: With our tongue we will be mighty; our lips are with us; who is master over us?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching from the same source: speaking לשון הרע is like denying God. It proves this from a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links speech to denying God. The people who say 'with our tongue we will be mighty' end by saying 'who is master over us?' This shows that loose, harmful speech comes from acting as if no one is in charge above you.

keyTerms.meaning: Denied the most basic belief, meaning belief in God

steps.whyThisMatters: This raises לשון הרע from a social wrong to something close to a denial of God.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן זִימְרָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra:
Anyone who speaks malicious speech
is as if he denied the fundamental belief,
as it says:
"Who have said: With our tongue we will be mighty;
our lips are with us;
who is master over us?"

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן זִימְרָא: כׇּל הַמְסַפֵּר לָשׁוֹן הָרָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same source on the same theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Speaking לשון הרע is as if one denied God.

steps.title: Speaking לשון הרע brings נגעים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בן זימרא teaches that one who speaks לשון הרע is struck with נגעים. He links the word אצמית in תהלים to לצמיתות in ויקרא, which the תרגום translates as לחלוטין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי בן זימרא said: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע, נגעים come upon him, as it says: 'Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will destroy him (אצמית).' And it is written there: 'in perpetuity (לצמיתות),' and we translate that as לחלוטין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third teaching: לשון הרע brings נגעים. It begins building the proof through a chain of word links, and the final link comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אצמית in the פסוק about slander shares a root with לצמיתות in the פסוק about selling land. The תרגום renders לצמיתות as לחלוטין, so the slanderer becomes 'מוחלט'. That word sets up the next step, where the משנה uses מוחלט for a confirmed מצורע.

keyTerms.meaning: Skin afflictions, the signs of צרעת
I will destroy him, or cut him off
Permanently, with certainty; the same root as מוחלט

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is not finished here. The word חלוטין only proves something once the next step shows that מוחלט is the term for a confirmed מצורע.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra said:
Anyone who speaks malicious speech,
leprous marks come upon him,
as it says:
"Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret,
I will destroy him."
And it is written there: "in perpetuity,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:23, about land not being sold permanently. It uses the same root as אצמית.

phrases.english: and we translate it: "permanently."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בֶּן זִימְרָא: כׇּל הַמְסַפֵּר לָשׁוֹן הָרָע, נְגָעִים בָּאִים עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third teaching on לשון הרע, this time naming its punishment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who speaks לשון הרע is struck with נגעים, proven through the link from אצמית to לצמיתות to לחלוטין.

steps.title: The משנה shows that מוחלט means a confirmed מצורע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה that uses the term מצורע מוחלט for a confirmed מצורע. This completes the chain: the slanderer described with the word אצמית, meaning חלוטין, is a מצורע מוחלט.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we learned in a משנה: The only difference between a quarantined מצורע and a confirmed מצורע is letting the hair grow wild and tearing the clothes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה to finish the proof from the last step. The משנה shows that מוחלט is the word used for a confirmed מצורע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 showed that the slanderer is called 'מוחלט'. This משנה shows that in the laws of צרעת, מוחלט means a person declared a definite מצורע, so the slanderer is struck with נגעים. The details about the hair and the clothes are not the point here. What matters is the term מוחלט.

keyTerms.meaning: A מצורע in quarantine, whose signs are not yet clear
A confirmed מצורע, declared definite by the כהן

steps.whatToRemember: The full chain: אצמית is like לצמיתות, which is translated חלוטין, which matches the משנה's מצורע מוחלט. So one who speaks לשון הרע gets צרעת.

phrases.english: And we learned in a משנה:
There is no difference between a quarantined leper
and a confirmed leper
except letting the hair grow wild and tearing the clothes.
phrases.notes: The confirmed מצורע must do these two things, and the quarantined one does not.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּתְנַן: אֵין בֵּין מְצוֹרָע מוּסְגָּר לִמְצוֹרָע מוּחְלָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the final link in the word chain that Step 7 began.
steps.raayaObject: That speaking לשון הרע brings נגעים, specifically confirmed צרעת
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's use of the term מצורע מוחלט, which matches the תרגום's word לחלוטין

steps.title: The law of the leper is the law of the slanderer
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש reads the פסוק about the מצורע as being about the מוציא שם רע.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says: What does the פסוק 'This shall be the law of the מצורע' mean? It means: this shall be the law of one who spreads a bad name about others.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains a פסוק in ויקרא. He says the purification laws of the מצורע are really the laws for a person who slanders others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said that a slanderer is struck with נגעים. Here ריש לקיש reads that idea straight into the Torah's own wording: the word מצורע hints at מוציא שם רע. The Torah's chapter on צרעת is really describing the slanderer.

keyTerms.meaning: A person struck with צרעת, a skin affliction
One who spreads a bad name or slander about someone
The law of, meaning the set of rules for

phrases.english: Reish Lakish says:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"This shall be the law of the leper"?
This shall be the law
of one who spreads a bad name.
phrases.notes: He's reading מצורע as if it said מוציא (שם) רע, because the two sound alike.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ריש לקיש מאי דכתיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the link between לשון הרע and צרעת from steps 7-8 with a new reading of a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah's law of the מצורע is the law of the מוציא שם רע.

steps.title: The animals ask the snake what it gains
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains a פסוק in קהלת with a parable. In the future, the animals ask the snake what benefit it gets from biting. The snake answers that a slanderer gains nothing either.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says: What does the פסוק 'If the snake bites without a charm, and there is no advantage to the master of the tongue' mean? In the future, all the animals will gather by the snake and say: A lion tramples its prey and eats it. A wolf tears its prey and eats it. But you, what pleasure do you get? The snake will answer: And what advantage does the slanderer get?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains why one פסוק mentions both a biting snake and a 'master of the tongue.' He tells a story about the future to connect the two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other predators kill in order to eat. The snake kills without getting anything out of it. When the animals challenge the snake, it points to the slanderer, who also harms people and gains nothing. This shows how pointless and evil לשון הרע is.

keyTerms.meaning: A charm or whispered spell, used to tame snakes
Master of the tongue, meaning one who speaks לשון הרע

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"If the serpent bites before it is charmed,
then there is no advantage to the master of the tongue"?
In the future,
all the animals will gather
and come to the serpent and say:
A lion tramples and eats;
a wolf tears and eats;
you, what benefit do you have?
It says to them:
And what is the benefit to the master of the tongue?

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמר ריש לקיש מאי דכתיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from ריש לקיש on the same theme of לשון הרע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The slanderer, like the snake, causes harm without gaining anything.

steps.title: Slander raises sins up to the heavens
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש teaches that one who speaks לשון הרע piles up sins as high as the heavens. He brings a proof from תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And ריש לקיש says: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע increases sins all the way to the heavens, as it says: 'They have set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walks through the earth.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a third teaching about how serious לשון הרע is, with a פסוק as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has the tongue walking on the earth while the mouth reaches the heavens. ריש לקיש reads this to mean that the words are spoken down here, but the sin they cause reaches all the way up.

keyTerms.meaning: One who speaks evil talk about others

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says:
Anyone who speaks malicious speech
increases sins until the heavens,
as it is stated: "They have set their mouth against the heavens,
and their tongue walks through the earth."

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמר ריש לקיש כל המספר לשון הרע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third teaching from ריש לקיש in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לשון הרע builds up sins as high as the heavens.

steps.title: A slanderer deserves to be stoned
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting מר עוקבא, teaches that a slanderer deserves stoning. He links the word אצמית in תהלים to צמתו in איכה, where stones are thrown.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא says in the name of מר עוקבא: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע deserves to be stoned. Here it says 'I will destroy (אצמית) him,' and there it says 'They have destroyed (צמתו) my life in the pit, and have cast stones upon me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא brings a new teaching from מר עוקבא. He links two פסוקים by a shared word to show that a slanderer deserves stoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the secret slanderer from step 7 uses the word אצמית. In איכה, a similar word, צמתו, describes being destroyed by stones. Because the same word appears in both, the destruction of the slanderer is understood as stoning.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written here and written there, used to link two פסוקים by a shared word

steps.whatToRemember: This section piles up teachings on how terrible לשון הרע is. It is the law of the מצורע, it is pointless like a snake's bite, it raises sins to the heavens, and it deserves stoning.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Deserves to be stoned' describes how severe the sin is. It does not mean a בית דין actually stones a slanderer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda says that Mar Ukva says:
Anyone who speaks malicious speech,
it is appropriate to stone him with stones.
It is written here: "Him I will destroy,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 101:5, the same פסוק about the secret slanderer we saw in step 7.

phrases.english: and it is written there:
"They have destroyed my life in the dungeon,
and have cast stones upon me."

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב חסדא אמר מר עוקבא כל המספר לשון הרע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new speaker adds another teaching about לשון הרע. It reuses the word אצמית from step 7, linked this time to stoning instead of נגעים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slanderer deserves stoning, learned through the word link between אצמית and צמתו.

steps.title: God cannot live in the world with a slanderer
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting מר עוקבא, teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא says He and the slanderer cannot live together in the world. He shows this by reading the פסוק in תהלים with a different vowel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע, God says about him: 'He and I cannot live together in the world.' The פסוק says, 'Whoever slanders his friend in secret, I will destroy him; the haughty and proud of heart, him I cannot bear.' Do not read 'him (אוֹתוֹ) I cannot bear.' Read it as 'with him (אִתּוֹ) I cannot be.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a second teaching in the name of מר עוקבא. It uses the same פסוק from Step 12: הקדוש ברוך הוא refuses to share the world with a person who speaks לשון הרע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from an אל תקרי, a 'do not read it this way, read it that way.' The word אותו (him) is reread as אתו (with him). So the פסוק does not only say 'I cannot bear him.' It says 'I cannot bear to be together with him.'

keyTerms.meaning: 'Do not read it as…'; the גמרא rereads a word in a פסוק with different vowels to learn a new idea

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not mean the פסוק is spelled wrong. The written letters stay the same. The גמרא is adding a second layer of meaning by reading the word with different vowels.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: And Rav Chisda said that Mar Ukva said:
Anyone who speaks evil speech,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, says:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אֲנִי וְהוּא יְכוֹלִין לָדוּר בָּעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: I and he cannot live together in the world,
as it is said: "Whoever slanders his friend in secret,
him I will destroy;
one with haughty eyes and a proud heart,
him I cannot bear."
Do not read "him I cannot bear,"
but rather "with him I cannot be."
phrases.notes: The letters stay the same and only the vowel changes: אוֹתוֹ means 'him' and אִתּוֹ means 'with him.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same pair, רב חסדא and מר עוקבא, based on the same פסוק in תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקדוש ברוך הוא cannot bear to live in the world together with one who speaks לשון הרע.

steps.title: Another version applies this to the arrogant
steps.stepSummary: Some teach this same idea, that God cannot live with him, about arrogant people instead of slanderers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some people teach this teaching about the arrogant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of the last teaching. In this version, the person God cannot live with is the arrogant person, not the slanderer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the words 'I cannot bear him' come right after 'haughty eyes and a proud heart.' So this version connects them to the arrogant person, who is mentioned closest to those words. The אל תקרי reading stays the same. Only the person it is about changes.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who teach it (another version of the teaching)
The arrogant, people with an inflated spirit

phrases.english: And there are those who teach it
about the arrogant.
phrases.notes: They connect 'I cannot live with him' to the end of the פסוק, 'proud of heart.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ עַל גַּסֵּי הָרוּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of Step 13 and changes who the teaching is about.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, God says He cannot live in the world with the arrogant.

steps.title: God and גיהנם judge the slanderer together
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting מר עוקבא, teaches that God tells גיהנם: 'I will judge him from above and you from below.' The proof begins with a פסוק about arrows, and 'arrow' is shown to mean the tongue.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע, God says to גיהנם, 'I am against him from above and you are against him from below. We will judge him together.' The פסוק says, 'Sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of broom-wood.' 'Arrow' always means the tongue, as it says, 'Their tongue is a sharpened arrow, it speaks deceit.'
steps.whatsHappening: A third teaching from רב חסדא in the name of מר עוקבא: the slanderer is punished from two sides at once. The גמרא begins to decode the proof פסוק one word at a time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof פסוק has three parts: arrows, mighty one, and coals. Here the גמרא decodes only the first: 'arrow' means the tongue, which is the sin of לשון הרע. The other two words are explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where the wicked are punished
'X means only Y'; a way of fixing what a word in a פסוק stands for

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Mar Ukva said:
Anyone who speaks evil speech,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, says to Gehinnom:
I will be against him from above
and you will be against him from below;
we will judge him.
phrases.notes: He means together, the two of them as a team.

phrases.english: As it is said: "Sharp arrows of the mighty one,
with coals of broom-wood."
"Arrow" means nothing other than the tongue,
as it is said: "Their tongue is a sharpened arrow,
it speaks deceit."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching in the same series from רב חסדא and מר עוקבא about the slanderer's punishment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God from above and גיהנם from below judge the slanderer together.

steps.title: Decoding 'mighty one' and 'coals'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes decoding the פסוק: 'mighty one' is God, and 'coals of broom-wood' is גיהנם.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Mighty one' always means God, as it says, 'ה׳ will go out like a mighty one.' 'Coals of broom-wood' means גיהנם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof from Step 15. It explains the last two words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the whole picture fits together. Arrows means the tongue, the sin. Mighty one means God, the judge from above. Coals means גיהנם, the punishment from below. So the פסוק describes exactly what the teaching said: God and גיהנם together punish the one whose tongue sinned.

keyTerms.meaning: Mighty one; here, הקדוש ברוך הוא

steps.whatToRemember: The slanderer's tongue is like an arrow. As a punishment, God from above and גיהנם from below judge him together.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין גִּבּוֹר אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: And "mighty one" means nothing other than the Holy One, Blessed be He,
as it is said: "ה׳ will go out like a mighty one."
"Coals of broom-wood": that is Gehinnom.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין גִּבּוֹר אֶלָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the word-by-word proof that Step 15 began.
steps.raayaObject: The teaching that God and גיהנם judge the slanderer together
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו 42:13 (גבור means God), together with the reading that גחלי רתמים means גיהנם

steps.title: The remedy for a תלמיד חכם: learning Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא asks what the fix is for people who speak לשון הרע. If the person is a תלמיד חכם, he should learn Torah, because the פסוק says Torah heals the tongue.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: What is the fix for people who speak לשון הרע? If he is a תלמיד חכם, let him learn Torah. The פסוק says, 'A healing for the tongue is a tree of life.' 'Tongue' means לשון הרע, as it says, 'Their tongue is a sharpened arrow.' 'Tree' means Torah, as it says, 'It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it.'
steps.whatsHappening: After all the frightening punishments, the גמרא turns to hope: how can a slanderer fix himself? This step gives the fix for a תלמיד חכם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is built from two word definitions. 'Tongue' means לשון הרע, and 'tree of life' means Torah. Put them together, and the פסוק says that Torah heals לשון הרע.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him busy himself with learning Torah
Tree of life; here, the Torah

steps.whyThisMatters: The section moves from punishment to repair. Even a sin as heavy as לשון הרע has a path back.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chama son of Rabbi Chanina said:

phrases.aramaic: מָה תַּקָּנָתוֹ שֶׁל מְסַפֵּרי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע?
phrases.english: What is the remedy for those who speak evil speech?
If he is a Torah scholar,
let him busy himself with Torah,
as it is said: "A healing for the tongue is a tree of life."
phrases.notes: משלי 15:4. The second half of this same פסוק comes up in the next step.

phrases.english: And "tongue" means nothing other than evil speech,
as it is said: "Their tongue is a sharpened arrow."
And "tree" means nothing other than Torah,
as it is said: "It is a tree of life to those who hold onto it."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מָה תַּקָּנָתוֹ שֶׁל מְסַפֵּרי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the slanderer's punishment to his remedy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם who spoke לשון הרע should fix it by learning Torah.

steps.title: The remedy for an עם הארץ: humbling himself
steps.stepSummary: If the slanderer is an עם הארץ, his fix is to humble himself, based on the second half of the same פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he is an unlearned person, let him humble himself. The פסוק says, 'And its crookedness is a breaking of the spirit.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא gives the second fix, for someone who cannot heal himself through Torah learning: humility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second half of משלי 15:4 talks about a crooked tongue and a 'broken spirit.' A person who twisted his tongue with לשון הרע can repair it by breaking his pride. The two halves of one פסוק give two remedies for two kinds of people.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him lower his mind, meaning become humble

steps.whatToRemember: The fix for לשון הרע: a תלמיד חכם should learn Torah, and an עם הארץ should humble himself. Both come from one פסוק, משלי 15:4.

phrases.english: And if he is an unlearned person,
let him humble his mind,
as it is said: "And its crookedness
is a breaking of the spirit."
phrases.notes: משלי 15:4. Some versions say רוח and some say ברוח; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם עַם הָאָרֶץ הוּא יַשְׁפִּיל דַּעְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי חמא ברבי חנינא's answer by giving the fix for the second kind of person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עם הארץ who spoke לשון הרע should fix it by humbling himself.

steps.title: Once spoken, לשון הרע has no fix
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא ברבי חנינא says that a person who already spoke לשון הרע has no remedy, because דוד already declared him cut off.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא ברבי חנינא says: If he already spoke it, he has no fix, because דוד, through רוח הקודש, already cut him off, as it says: 'May God cut off all smooth lips, the tongue that speaks great things.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא, רבי אחא ברבי חנינא, gives a harsher view: once the לשון הרע has been said, it can't be fixed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads the word יכרת in the פסוק as a statement of punishment, not just a wish. דוד said it with רוח הקודש, so the decree stands. This seems to clash with the remedy we just learned in steps 17-18.

keyTerms.meaning: Will cut off, from the same root as כָּרֵת

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי אחא is arguing that there is no remedy at all. He means there's no fix after the words are spoken. The next step shows his remedy is preventive, for before it happens.

phrases.english: Rabbi Acha son of Rabbi Chanina says:
If he already spoke it, he has no fix,
because David already cut him off through Divine inspiration,
as it says: "May God cut off all smooth lips,
the tongue that speaks great things."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַחָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different, stricter view after רבי חמא's remedy in steps 17-18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once לשון הרע is spoken, there is no remedy, because דוד already decreed כרת on it.

steps.title: The remedy is prevention: Torah or humility
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא explains that the fix is to prevent לשון הרע ahead of time: a תלמיד חכם learns Torah, and an עם הארץ humbles himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what is his fix so that he does not come to speak לשון הרע? If he is a Torah scholar, he should learn Torah. If he is unlearned, he should humble himself, as it says: 'and its crookedness, a breaking in the spirit.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אחא continues and says the real fix works only beforehand, to keep a person from speaking לשון הרע at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He gives the same two remedies that רבי חמא gave in steps 17-18, but he changes their purpose. For רבי חמא they fix the sin. For רבי אחא they only prevent it. A broken, humble spirit protects against the 'crookedness' of the tongue.

keyTerms.meaning: He should humble himself, lower his self-importance

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי אחא, Torah study and humility don't erase לשון הרע already spoken. They are a shield that keeps you from speaking it.

phrases.english: Rather, what is his fix
so that he does not come to speak לשון הרע?

phrases.aramaic: אִם תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הוּא יַעֲסוֹק בַּתּוֹרָה,
phrases.english: If he is a Torah scholar, he should learn Torah,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם עַם הָאָרֶץ הוּא יַשְׁפִּיל דַּעְתּוֹ,
phrases.english: and if he is unlearned, he should humble himself,
as it says: "and its crookedness, a breaking in the spirit."
phrases.notes: משלי 15:4. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מָה תַּקָּנָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יָבֹא לִידֵי לָשׁוֹן הָרָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי אחא's statement by turning the remedy into prevention.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: To avoid לשון הרע, a תלמיד חכם should learn Torah and an עם הארץ should humble himself.

steps.title: לשון הרע equals the three worst sins
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל teaches that לשון הרע is as bad as עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים, and starts the proof with the word 'great'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: Anyone who speaks לשון הרע makes his sins as great as the three sins of idol worship, forbidden relations, and murder. It says here: 'a tongue that speaks great things,' and about idol worship it says: 'Please, this people has sinned a great sin.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching says לשון הרע is as serious as all three of the worst sins. The proof begins by linking the word 'great' in the לשון הרע פסוק to the word 'great' used for עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof works by matching words. The לשון הרע פסוק says 'great things', in the plural. Each of the three big sins is called 'great' in the singular somewhere in the Torah. Here the גמרא gives the first one, עבודה זרה at the golden calf.

keyTerms.meaning: Increases sins, makes the sin grow
It is written here, used to set up a word-comparison between פסוקים

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Anyone who speaks לשון הרע
makes his sins as great as three sins:

phrases.aramaic: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְגִילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת וּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים.
phrases.english: idol worship, forbidden relations, and murder.
It is written here: "a tongue that speaks great things,"
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק from step 19, תהלים 12:4. Notice that 'great things' is plural.

phrases.english: and it is written about idol worship:
"Please, this people has sinned a great sin."
phrases.notes: שמות 32:31, משה speaking about the golden calf.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק about 'great things' from step 19 to make a new point about how severe לשון הרע is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לשון הרע is as severe as עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים.

steps.title: 'Great' for forbidden relations and for murder
steps.stepSummary: The proof is finished: the Torah also calls גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים 'great' in the singular.
steps.simpleTranslation: About forbidden relations it says: 'How can I do this great evil?' About murder it says: 'My sin is too great to bear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof by showing that the other two big sins are also called 'great'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now all three sins have a singular 'great'. Since לשון הרע gets the plural 'great things', it adds up to all of them together.

keyTerms.meaning: The great evil, said by יוסף
My sin is too great to bear, said by קין

steps.whatToRemember: Singular 'great' appears for each of the three worst sins, and plural 'great things' appears for לשון הרע. That is why לשון הרע is compared to all three.

phrases.english: About forbidden relations it is written:
"How can I do this great evil?"
About murder it is written:
"My sin is too great to bear."

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּגִילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the word-comparison that began in step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That לשון הרע equals all three of the worst sins
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 39:9 and בראשית 4:13, where 'great' describes גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים

steps.title: Maybe the plural only means two
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the plural 'great things' only proves a minimum of two, so maybe לשון הרע equals just two of the sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Great things' — say it means only two!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. A plural word only has to mean two, so why say לשון הרע equals all three sins?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a plural word proves at least two, not more. So the word 'גדולות' seems to show only that לשון הרע equals two of the three sins.

phrases.english: "Great things": say it means only two!

steps.triggerLanguage: גְּדוֹלוֹת אֵימָא תַּרְתֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof from steps 21-22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that plural 'גדולות' makes לשון הרע equal to all three sins
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A plural only proves a minimum of two, so at most two sins are proven.

steps.title: None of the three can be left out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: which of the three would you remove? They are equally severe, so all three must be included.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which of them would you take out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a short question: which sin could you leave out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three sins are equally serious, and each one is called 'great'. There is no reason to drop any of them, so 'great things' must cover all three.
steps.whatToRemember: The final point: לשון הרע is as serious as עבודה זרה, גילוי עריות and שפיכות דמים all together.

phrases.english: Which of them would you take out?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי מִינַּיְיהוּ מַפְּקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rhetorical question showing there is no basis to exclude any of the three
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Plural 'גדולות' might mean only two of the sins.
steps.terutzMaskana: No sin can be singled out to exclude, so לשון הרע equals all three.

steps.title: Harmful speech kills three people
steps.stepSummary: In ארץ ישראל they teach that לשון הרע about a third person kills three: the speaker, the listener who accepts it, and the person spoken about.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the West they say: speech about a third person kills three people. It kills the one who tells it, the one who accepts it, and the one it is said about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a saying from ארץ ישראל that shows how much damage לשון הרע does: it harms three people at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds to the earlier teaching that לשון הרע equals the three worst sins. The new point is the reach of the harm. It destroys the speaker and the listener who believes it, not only the victim.

keyTerms.meaning: 'In the West': ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל
'Third speech': talk about a third person who is not present
The one who tells the לשון הרע
The one who accepts and believes the לשון הרע

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that listening to and believing לשון הרע is also deadly, not just saying it.

phrases.english: In the West they say:
Third speech kills three,
phrases.notes: 'Third speech' means talk about a third person, someone other than the speaker and the listener.

phrases.english: it kills the one who tells it,
and the one who accepts it,
and the one about whom it is said.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַעְרְבָא אָמְרִי: לָשׁוֹן תְּלִיתַאי קָטֵיל תְּלִיתַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another teaching about the severity of לשון הרע after the proof that it equals the three cardinal sins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לשון הרע harms three people: the speaker, the listener who accepts it, and the subject.

steps.title: The tongue can kill like a hand
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא explains that the פסוק says 'in the hand of the tongue' to teach that a tongue can kill just as a hand can.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: What is the meaning of the פסוק 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue'? Does a tongue have a hand? It comes to teach you that just as a hand can kill, a tongue can also kill.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא points out a strange phrase in a פסוק, 'the hand of the tongue', and explains that it compares the tongue to a hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tongue has no hand, so the word 'hand' must be teaching something. It teaches that the tongue has the deadly power of a hand. This comparison will be tested in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is that which is written?': asking for the meaning of a פסוק
'Is there really…?': pointing out that something in the פסוק cannot be literal
'To tell you': introducing the lesson the פסוק comes to teach

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥama son of Rabbi Ḥanina said:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"Death and life are in the hand of the tongue"?
Does the tongue have a hand?
It is to tell you:
just as a hand kills,
so too a tongue kills.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מַאי דִּכְתִיב ״מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד לָשׁוֹן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new teaching that brings פסוקים showing how deadly the tongue is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tongue can kill, just like a hand.

steps.title: Maybe the tongue kills only close by, like a hand
steps.stepSummary: The comparison to a hand might suggest that the tongue can kill only someone nearby.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so: just as a hand kills only someone close to it, maybe a tongue also kills only someone close to it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא continues his own derivation and pushes the hand comparison further and asks whether it limits the tongue's power to nearby people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the tongue is like a hand in every way, it should share the hand's limits too. A hand can only reach someone right next to it. This possible limit needs to be ruled out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If, just as…': testing whether a comparison carries over in every detail

phrases.english: If: just as a hand kills only
someone close to it,
so too a tongue kills
only someone close to it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מָה יָד אֵינָהּ מְמִיתָה אֶלָּא בְּסָמוּךְ לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the hand comparison from step 26 should be taken.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of the tongue to a hand
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the tongue is like a hand, it should share the hand's limit of killing only nearby.

steps.title: The tongue is like an arrow
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק calls the tongue a sharpened arrow, so it kills from a distance.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why the פסוק says: 'Their tongue is a sharpened arrow.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא answers with a second פסוק, which compares the tongue to an arrow that hits from far away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An arrow kills from a distance, unlike a hand. So the arrow פסוק removes the 'close by only' limit. The tongue can harm someone far away from the speaker.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The פסוק teaches': bringing a פסוק to settle the question

phrases.english: Therefore the פסוק says:
"Their tongue is a sharpened arrow."

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״חֵץ שָׁחוּט לְשׁוֹנָם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tongue kills only nearby, like a hand.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tongue kills from a distance, like an arrow.

steps.title: Maybe the tongue reaches only as far as an arrow
steps.stepSummary: An arrow reaches only about forty or fifty אמות, so maybe the tongue's reach is limited the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so: just as an arrow reaches only forty or fifty אמות, maybe a tongue also reaches only forty or fifty אמות?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the new arrow comparison the same way: maybe the tongue also shares the arrow's limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repeats the move of step 27. Each comparison brings its own limit. An arrow can only fly a certain distance, so the tongue might be limited to that range.

keyTerms.meaning: A cubit, a measure of length of about half a meter

phrases.aramaic: אִי מָה חֵץ עַד אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה,
phrases.english: If: just as an arrow reaches up to forty or fifty cubits,

phrases.aramaic: אַף לָשׁוֹן עַד אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה?
phrases.english: so too a tongue reaches only up to forty or fifty cubits?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מָה חֵץ עַד אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the arrow comparison from step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of the tongue to an arrow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the tongue is like an arrow, it should share the arrow's limited range.

steps.title: The tongue reaches from heaven to earth
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק in תהלים shows that the tongue's reach has no such limit. It stretches from heaven to earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why the פסוק says: 'They have set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walks through the earth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a third פסוק, which shows that the tongue reaches everywhere, from heaven down to earth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mouth is in the heavens while the tongue travels on the earth. So the tongue's reach covers the whole distance between heaven and earth. This removes the arrow's limit.

phrases.english: Therefore the פסוק says:
"They have set their mouth against the heavens,
and their tongue walks through the earth."

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״שַׁתּוּ בַשָּׁמַיִם פִּיהֶם וּלְשׁוֹנָם תִּהֲלַךְ בָּאָרֶץ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 29.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The tongue reaches only as far as an arrow flies.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tongue's harm reaches from heaven to earth.

steps.title: Why is the arrow פסוק needed at all?
steps.stepSummary: The heaven-and-earth פסוק already teaches unlimited reach, so the גמרא asks what the arrow פסוק adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since it is written 'They have set their mouth against the heavens', why do I need 'Their tongue is a sharpened arrow'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks back and asks whether the arrow פסוק is extra, since the last פסוק already covers everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heaven-and-earth פסוק proves that the tongue reaches far, even farther than an arrow. So the arrow פסוק seems to teach nothing new about distance. The גמרא wants to know its purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Since it is written': one פסוק already teaches this
'Why do I need it?': asking what an apparently extra source adds

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an attack on the lesson itself. The גמרא agrees the tongue reaches far. It only asks what the arrow פסוק adds.

phrases.english: But since it is written:
"They have set their mouth against the heavens,"
why do I need "Their tongue is a sharpened arrow"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דִּכְתִיב ״שַׁתּוּ בַּשָּׁמַיִם פִּיהֶם״, ״חֵץ שָׁחוּט לְשׁוֹנָם״ לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the arrow פסוק from step 28 is extra after step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק 'חֵץ שָׁחוּט לְשׁוֹנָם'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The heaven-and-earth פסוק already proves unlimited reach, so the arrow פסוק looks extra.

steps.title: The arrow teaches how the tongue kills
steps.stepSummary: The arrow פסוק teaches the manner of killing: the tongue kills the way an arrow does.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us that the tongue kills like an arrow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the arrow פסוק is not about distance. It teaches the way the tongue kills, like an arrow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heaven-and-earth פסוק teaches how far the tongue reaches. The arrow פסוק teaches what kind of damage it does: it strikes and kills like an arrow. So each פסוק has its own job.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This teaches us': explaining the special point a source adds

steps.whatToRemember: The tongue kills like a hand, it kills like an arrow, and it reaches from heaven to earth. Every פסוק adds its own part of the lesson about how deadly לשון הרע is.

phrases.english: This teaches us
that it kills like an arrow.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָמַשְׁמַע לַן, דְּקָטֵיל כְּחֵץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives each פסוק its own lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The arrow פסוק is extra once the heaven-and-earth פסוק teaches distance.
steps.terutzMaskana: The arrow פסוק teaches the manner of killing, like an arrow.

steps.title: Why do we need the 'death and life' verse?
steps.stepSummary: The arrow פסוק already teaches that the tongue kills, so the גמרא asks what the פסוק in משלי adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it already says 'Their tongue is a sharpened arrow,' why do we need the verse 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a second פסוק about the tongue's power to kill is needed. The arrow פסוק already told us that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 showed that the arrow פסוק teaches how the tongue kills. So the פסוק in משלי, which also says the tongue can kill, looks extra. The גמרא wants to know what new thing it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: In the hand of the tongue, meaning in the tongue's power

phrases.english: But since it is written
"Their tongue is a sharpened arrow"
"Death and life are in the hand of the tongue"
why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the pattern from step 31: once one פסוק teaches something, a second פסוק that seems to repeat it is challenged.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק in משלי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The arrow פסוק already teaches that the tongue kills, so a second פסוק saying the same thing looks unnecessary.

steps.title: The tongue can bring life or death
steps.stepSummary: The משלי פסוק teaches רבא's idea: a person can earn life or death through how he uses his tongue.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for רבא's teaching. רבא said: whoever wants life gets it through his tongue, and whoever wants death gets it through his tongue.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משלי פסוק teaches something new. The tongue does not only kill. It can also bring life to the speaker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The arrow פסוק is only about harm done to others. The משלי פסוק adds 'life' and focuses on the speaker himself. Good speech, like learning Torah, earns life, and bad speech earns death.
steps.whatToRemember: Both פסוקים are needed. The arrow פסוק teaches how the tongue kills others. The משלי פסוק teaches that the speaker's own life or death depends on his speech.

phrases.english: It is needed for רבא's teaching, as רבא says:
One who wants life gets it through his tongue
One who wants death gets it through his tongue.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְכִדְרָבָא, דְּאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns a separate teaching to the seemingly extra פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משלי פסוק only repeats that the tongue can kill.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משלי פסוק teaches that the speaker's own life or death depends on his speech.

steps.title: What exactly is harmful speech?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a definition of לישנא בישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does לישנא בישא look like?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It asks what kind of speech actually counts as לישנא בישא, and the next steps will answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the sugya talked about how dangerous לישנא בישא is. Now it asks where the line is drawn.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? what does it look like?
harmful speech, speaking badly about others

phrases.english: What is considered harmful speech?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the פסוקים about the tongue to defining the sin itself.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A working definition of לישנא בישא

steps.title: רבא's example: 'There is fire at so-and-so's house'
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that saying 'there is always fire at so-and-so's house' is לישנא בישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: for example, if someone says, 'There is fire at so-and-so's house.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives an example. Even a simple remark that someone is always cooking counts as לישנא בישא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The remark hints that the family eats a lot or lives in luxury. רבא sees even this mild hint as forbidden speech.

phrases.english: רבא said: For example, if one says
"There is fire at so-and-so's house."
phrases.notes: He means a fire is always going there, so they are always cooking.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Even a plain report that someone's fire is always burning counts as לישנא בישא.

steps.title: אביי: that is just stating a fact
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects that simply saying there is fire somewhere only reports a fact.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: What did he do wrong? He is just telling over a fact!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on רבא's example. He says that just reporting a true fact is not harmful speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's example looks like a neutral sentence with no negative tone. אביי argues that this cannot be enough to count as לישנא בישא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי קָא עָבֵיד?
phrases.english: אביי said to him: What did he do wrong?
He is merely revealing a fact!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי קָא עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's example in step 36.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A neutral, true report has nothing harmful in it, so it should not count as forbidden speech.

steps.title: It is forbidden when said in a mocking way
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that it becomes לישנא בישא when said with a negative spin: 'Where else is there fire, except at so-and-so's?'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is when he says it in a harmful way, saying: 'Where can you find fire, except at so-and-so's house?'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives his own, sharper version of the example. The speech becomes forbidden because of its mocking tone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The facts are the same as in רבא's example. What changes is the tone. 'Where else is there fire except at so-and-so's' makes fun of the family as people who always eat. That tone is what makes the speech harmful.

keyTerms.meaning: who expresses it, brings it out

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, the same fact can be fine or forbidden. It depends on whether it is said in a mocking, negative way.

phrases.english: Rather, it is when he expresses it in a harmful way,
saying: "Where can fire be found
except at so-and-so's house?"

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּמַפֵּיק בְּלִישָּׁנָא בִּישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: אביי replaces רבא's example after his challenge in step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so that the tone makes it forbidden
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any mention of someone's fire, even neutral, is לישנא בישא.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is לישנא בישא only when said in a mocking, negative way.

steps.title: רבה: speech in front of the person is not לישנא בישא
steps.stepSummary: רבה rules that anything said in the presence of the person it is about does not count as לישנא בישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Anything said in front of the person it is about does not count as לישנא בישא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה makes a new rule about לישנא בישא. If the person is right there, it is not considered harmful speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's idea seems to be that לישנא בישא is talking behind someone's back. When the person hears it and can answer, it falls outside the category.

keyTerms.meaning: in front of its owner, the person it is about
it does not have the problem of

phrases.english: רבה says: Any statement
that is said in the presence of its owner,
phrases.notes: Literally 'its master,' meaning the person the statement is about.

phrases.english: does not have any problem of harmful speech.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: כֹּל מִילְּתָא דְּמִיתְאַמְרָא בְּאַפֵּי מָרַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another boundary to the definition of לישנא בישא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Speech said in the presence of its subject is not לישנא בישא.

steps.title: Even worse: it is both rude and harmful
steps.stepSummary: רבה is challenged: saying it to his face is worse, because it is both חוצפא and לישנא בישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: All the more so! It is both חוצפא and לישנא בישא!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's rule. He argues that saying bad things to a person's face should be worse, not allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger turns רבה's reasoning upside down. Saying it openly keeps the harmful speech and adds a new sin, brazen rudeness.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבה is saying it is fine to insult people to their face. He only claims it is not the specific sin of לישנא בישא, and the challenger disagrees.

phrases.english: He said to him: All the more so
it is both brazenness and harmful speech!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן חוּצְפָּא וְלִישָּׁנָא בִּישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's rule from step 39.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that speech in front of the person is not לישנא בישא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying it to his face does not remove the harm. It adds חוצפא, so it should be worse.

steps.title: רבה relies on רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that he follows רבי יוסי, who never said anything he would worry about the person overhearing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I hold like רבי יוסי, as רבי יוסי said: In all my days I never said something and then looked behind me. He says...
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends his rule with the behavior of רבי יוסי. רבי יוסי only said things he would be willing to say in front of the person himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי never had to check whether the person was behind him, because he would have said it to his face anyway. This shows that speech one is willing to say openly is not considered harmful speech. That is רבה's point.

keyTerms.meaning: I hold, this is my view
I turned to look behind me

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical test for speech: would you say it if the person were standing right behind you?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי סְבִירָא לִי,
phrases.english: He said to him: I hold like רבי יוסי,
as רבי יוסי says:
In all my days I never said something
and then turned to look behind me.
phrases.notes: He never had to check if the person was listening, because he would have said it to his face anyway.

phrases.english: He says,
phrases.notes: This word opens a new statement by a different sage, which continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי סְבִירָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבה answers the challenge of step 40.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeals to an earlier authority's practice
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Speaking in front of the person only adds חוצפא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Speech a person would openly say in front of the subject is not לישנא בישא, as seen from רבי יוסי.
